summary_profile.description: Tuberculosis (TB) is a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It most commonly affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can also involve other organs such as lymph nodes, spine, brain, kidneys, or bones (extrapulmonary TB). TB spreads through airborne droplets when an infected person coughs, speaks, or sneezes. It can remain latent (inactive) in the body for years without causing symptoms. Without proper treatment, active TB can be fatal, but it is curable with timely diagnosis and a full course of antibiotics.
common_symptoms: Persistent cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks
Low-grade fever, especially in the evening
severe_symptoms: Severe shortness of breath or respiratory distress
Chest pain that worsens with breathing
Confusion or altered mental status (if TB meningitis)
Severe back pain or neurological weakness (spinal TB)
causes: Airborne transmission through droplets from infected persons
Close and prolonged contact with active TB patients
Reactivation of latent TB infection when immunity drops
risk_factors: HIV/AIDS (greatly increases risk of active TB)
Living in crowded or poorly ventilated conditions
Close contact with active TB cases
Recent travel to or living in high-burden countries
diagnosis_methods: GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rapid PCR test — detects TB and rifampicin resistance)
Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) or Mantoux test
treatment_options: Longer regimens (9–20 months) for Drug-Resistant TB
Hospitalization for severe cases or complications
medications: For Drug-Resistant TB: Bedaquiline, Delamanid, Linezolid, Clofazimine, etc.
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) — to prevent nerve damage from Isoniazid
lifestyle_home_remedies: Complete the full course of medication without interruption
Cover mouth and nose while coughing/sneezing
Isolation during the initial infectious period
diet_recommended: High-protein diet (eggs, milk, dal, fish, chicken, nuts)
Fresh fruits and vegetables rich in vitamins (especially Vitamin A, C, D)
Garlic, ginger, and turmeric (natural immune boosters)
complications: Lung cavitation and permanent lung damage
summary_profile.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor if you have a persistent cough for more than 2–3 weeks, especially with fever, night sweats, weight loss, or if you have been in contact with a TB patient. Early diagnosis saves lives.
emergency_signs: Coughing up large amounts of blood
Confusion, seizures, or neck stiffness (possible TB meningitis)
Severe weight loss with extreme weakness
